title: Medical Consultant: Bootstrap CI for a Proportion

steps.instruction: The consultant had **3 complications in 62 surgeries** (p̂ = 0.048), versus a national rate of **10%**. You'll bootstrap a 95% confidence interval for her true rate. **Before you start, commit to a prediction.**

gate.question: Where do you think the 95% bootstrap CI will fall relative to the national 10%?

choices.text: It will include 10% — we won't be able to rule out the national rate
It will sit entirely below 10% — clear evidence she's better

gate.feedback: With only 62 patients the CI is wide and its upper bound lands right around 10% — so 10% is **not** ruled out. A small sample can't separate 'genuinely better' from 'lucky.' Now bootstrap it and see.
gate.retryFeedback: Think about how wide a CI built from just 62 observations (3 complications) will be.

steps.instruction: Click **+1** several times and watch the resampled proportion after each click.
steps.observe: Does the proportion change each time? Does it ever hit exactly 3/62 (0.048)? Does it ever reach 0? Does it get as high as 0.10 (the national average)?
steps.reveal: Because we resample with replacement, each resample is different. With only 3 complications in 62 patients, most resamples have 2, 3, or 4 complications. Proportions near 0 are possible. Reaching 0.10 (about 6 complications) is less common but possible.

steps.instruction: Click the **Play** button and watch the bootstrap distribution build, then **Pause** and click **+1000**.
steps.observe: Read the **95% CI** bounds. Is 0.10 (the national complication rate) inside the interval, outside it, or right on the boundary?
steps.reveal: The upper bound of the 95% CI is near 0.10 — it may just barely include or exclude it depending on the number of resamples. This is a borderline case. Either way, we don't have strong evidence that the consultant's rate is truly lower than average. The sample is small (n = 62) and the CI is wide, so complication rates anywhere from 0% up to around 10% are plausible.

steps.instruction: You've bootstrapped the consultant's complication rate. Put the key ideas in your own words.

prompts.label: Given the 95% CI includes 10%, can we conclude the consultant's rate is no different from the national rate — or only that we can't rule it out?
Why does small-sample discreteness make the borderline-vs-clear-cut distinction harder here than at n = 620?
What one change to the study design would give the strongest chance of demonstrating a real improvement?
